title: Customer Support Resolution Agent
summary: Design an AI-powered customer support agent that handles inquiries, resolves issues, and escalates complex cases. Tests Agent SDK usage, MCP tools, deterministic enforcement, and escalation logic.
focus: Agentic loop control via stop_reason
Pre-execution hooks for deterministic enforcement
Tool description quality for reliable tool selection
Escalation triggers (the three valid ones)
Case-facts blocks for context preservation

decisions.q: How should the agentic loop terminate?
decisions.correct: Inspect stop_reason — continue on "tool_use" (run tools, append results, loop), terminate on "end_turn".
decisions.anti: Parsing assistant text for completion phrases like "done" or "complete"; or checking response.content[0].type == "text".

decisions.q: How to enforce a £500 refund limit so it can never be exceeded?
decisions.correct: Pre-execution tool-call interception hook (a prerequisite gate) that BLOCKS process_refund when amount > £500 before the tool fires, routing those calls to a human approval workflow.
decisions.anti: A PostToolUse hook — it runs AFTER execution, so the refund has already been processed by the time the hook fires. Equally wrong: relying on "never exceed £500" in the system prompt.

decisions.q: The agent frequently calls get_customer for order-status questions like "check my order #12345" instead of lookup_order. Both tools have minimal, near-identical descriptions. What's the highest-leverage first fix?
decisions.correct: Expand each tool's description with input formats, example queries, and explicit boundaries (e.g. "lookup_order: order status/tracking given an order ID — not for customer profile or billing details"). Tool descriptions are the primary signal the model uses for selection.
decisions.anti: Jumping straight to 5-8 few-shot examples (token overhead without fixing the root cause) or building a keyword-based routing layer (over-engineered, bypasses the model's own reasoning) before trying better descriptions.

decisions.q: When should the agent escalate to a human?
decisions.correct: On the three valid triggers: explicit human request (immediate, no "let me try first"), policy gaps requiring human judgement, or genuine inability to make progress after attempting resolution.
decisions.anti: Escalating on negative sentiment, frustration cues, or self-reported low confidence — sentiment doesn't correlate with case complexity, and LLM confidence isn't calibrated.

decisions.q: How to preserve customer details in a long, multi-turn conversation that gets summarised?
decisions.correct: A persistent case-facts block at the start of every prompt holding customer ID, order numbers, amounts, dates — never summarised, always present.
decisions.anti: Progressive summarisation that silently loses specifics (refund amount, order number, dates) round by round.

domainsTested: D1: Agentic loop control via stop_reason
D1: Pre-execution hooks for deterministic enforcement (NOT PostToolUse)
D2: Tool description quality as the primary tool-selection signal (expand before few-shot or routing layers)
D5: Escalation triggers (three valid; sentiment/confidence invalid)
D5: Case-facts blocks for context preservation
strategy: Watch for the PostToolUse-for-blocking trap on the £500 refund question — it's the wrong direction. Pre-execution interception is the only deterministic way to block. When two tools get confused, fix descriptions before reaching for few-shot examples or a routing layer. On escalation, reject sentiment- and confidence-based triggers in favour of explicit-request / policy-gap / can't-progress.

title: Code Generation with Claude Code
summary: Configure Claude Code for a development team's workflow. Tests CLAUDE.md hierarchy, skills vs commands, plan-vs-direct mode selection, and iterative refinement.
focus: CLAUDE.md hierarchy (user vs project vs directory; .claude/rules path-scoping)
Skills vs commands; .claude/skills/ frontmatter options
Plan mode vs direct execution (driven by ambiguity, not difficulty)
Iterative refinement: concrete examples vs interview pattern vs test-driven
Avoiding stale context when resuming a session after file edits

decisions.q: Where should team-wide coding standards live?
decisions.correct: .claude/CLAUDE.md (or root CLAUDE.md) — project-level, version-controlled, shared via git on clone.
decisions.anti: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (user-level, personal only — the famous "new-team-member trap" where new devs never receive the team conventions).

decisions.q: When to use plan mode versus direct execution?
decisions.correct: Decide by AMBIGUITY, not difficulty. Plan mode for multi-file architectural changes, codebase exploration, or multiple valid approaches. Direct execution for well-scoped, well-understood fixes (e.g. a single-function bug with a clear stack trace).
decisions.anti: Always using plan mode (wasteful) or never using it (risky for complex changes). Don't equate "hard" with "needs plan mode" — a hard but well-defined task can still go direct.

decisions.q: How to handle a verbose skill that would pollute the main session's context?
decisions.correct: Define it under .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md with `context: fork` in the frontmatter — the skill runs in an isolated sub-agent and only the summary returns to the main session.
decisions.anti: A plain `.claude/commands/<name>.md` (no frontmatter) that runs in the main session and floods context with verbose exploration output.

decisions.q: Best iterative refinement strategy when prose instructions yield inconsistent outputs?
decisions.correct: Provide 2–4 CONCRETE input/output examples (few-shot) that demonstrate the exact transformation; use the interview pattern instead when you're in an unfamiliar DOMAIN; escalate to test-driven iteration for complex transformations with many edge cases.
decisions.anti: More verbose prose instructions ("be more careful"). Prose is the source of the inconsistency — adding more of it doesn't fix interpretation drift.

decisions.q: After editing 3 of 50 files across two work sessions, you `--resume` and ask Claude to re-read the changed files. It still references old function signatures and re-recommends fixes already applied. What's actually wrong, and what's the fix?
decisions.correct: Stale context: --resume restores the ENTIRE prior history, including old tool-read file contents, which keep influencing reasoning even after a re-read. Fix: start a fresh session, inject a structured summary of prior findings plus the list of changed files, then do a TARGETED re-analysis of just those files.
decisions.anti: Assuming a re-read alone clears stale data (it doesn't — old results remain in history), or using fork_session to "solve" it — a fork inherits the same stale history, so it doesn't help either.

domainsTested: D3: CLAUDE.md hierarchy and the user-vs-project trap
D3: .claude/skills/ frontmatter (context: fork, allowed-tools, argument-hint)
D3: Plan vs direct by ambiguity, not difficulty
D3: Concrete examples vs interview pattern vs test-driven refinement
D5: Stale context after --resume; fresh start + summary + targeted re-analysis
strategy: The exam loves to test the user-vs-project trap. Memorise: team-wide → project; personal → user. For plan-vs-direct, ambiguity is the criterion (not file count, not difficulty). For inconsistent output, examples first — only escalate when you need them. If a resumed session contradicts itself after edits, that's stale context — fresh start + summary + targeted re-analysis, not a naive re-read or fork_session.

title: Multi-Agent Research System
summary: Build a coordinator-subagent system for parallel research tasks. Tests hub-and-spoke orchestration, subagent context isolation, error propagation, and information provenance.
focus: Hub-and-spoke architecture and centralised communication
Subagent context isolation
Scoped tool distribution across specialised subagents
Structured error propagation (no silent suppression, no workflow termination)
Information provenance and conflict handling

decisions.q: What architecture for parallel research tasks?
decisions.correct: Hub-and-spoke: a coordinator decomposes the task and delegates to specialised subagents; ALL inter-subagent communication flows through the coordinator.
decisions.anti: Direct subagent-to-subagent communication "for efficiency". It breaks observability, consistent error handling, and controlled information flow.

decisions.q: What context does each subagent see from the coordinator?
decisions.correct: Only what the coordinator explicitly puts in that subagent's prompt — passed as structured findings (claim + source URL + document + date) where relevant.
decisions.anti: The full coordinator conversation history. Subagents have fully isolated context by design — assuming inheritance produces silent failures.

decisions.q: The synthesis subagent frequently needs to verify simple facts (dates, names, statistics) while combining findings — every check currently round-trips through the coordinator to the web-search agent, adding latency. 85% of checks are simple lookups; 15% need deep investigation. What's the most effective fix?
decisions.correct: Give the synthesis agent a narrowly scoped verify_fact tool for the common simple-lookup case, while complex verifications continue routing through the coordinator to the web-search agent as before — apply least privilege, don't over-provision.
decisions.anti: Granting the synthesis agent full web-search tool access (over-provisioning, breaks separation of concerns) or batching all verification needs to the end of its pass (creates blocking dependencies when later steps depend on earlier verified facts).

decisions.q: How to handle conflicting data from different subagents?
decisions.correct: Preserve provenance for every claim (source URL, document name, publication date). When two credible sources disagree, annotate BOTH values with attribution and dates — the difference is often a real trend, not a data-quality issue.
decisions.anti: Arbitrarily choosing the most recent (or averaging) without surfacing the conflict to the reader.

decisions.q: How to handle a subagent failure (e.g. timeout)?
decisions.correct: Return structured error context: failure type, what was attempted, any partial results, and alternative approaches. The coordinator then chooses to retry, try an alternative, proceed with partials (with coverage annotations), or escalate.
decisions.anti: Silent suppression (empty results marked success) or workflow termination on the first failure — both destroy recovery options.

domainsTested: D1: Hub-and-spoke orchestration
D1: Subagent context isolation
D2: Scoped cross-role tool access (least privilege) for high-frequency needs
D5: Structured error propagation
D5: Information provenance and conflict annotation
strategy: This is the hardest scenario. Four traps to watch: (1) any decision that lets subagents talk directly is wrong; (2) over-provisioning a subagent's tools (e.g. full web-search access) to save round-trips violates least privilege — a narrow scoped tool for the common case is the answer; (3) any "empty results marked success" pattern is silent suppression; (4) any single-value answer in a multi-source conflict question is wrong — annotate both with provenance.

title: Developer Productivity with Claude
summary: Build developer tools using the Claude Agent SDK with built-in tools and MCP servers. Tests tool selection, MCP configuration, codebase exploration, and the Edit / Read+Write fallback ordering.
focus: Agentic loop control for autonomous multi-step exploration
Built-in tool selection (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob)
MCP server configuration and ${ENV_VAR} secret handling
Tool distribution (4–5 per agent; scoped cross-role tools)
Edit recovery: widen anchor / replace_all before Read+Write
Plan mode for multi-file migrations with several valid approaches

decisions.q: You're building an agent that autonomously explores a legacy codebase, decides which files to inspect next, and synthesises a migration plan across many decision points. What loop-control approach keeps it reliable?
decisions.correct: A stop_reason-driven agentic loop: keep running tools while stop_reason is "tool_use" (appending each tool result to history so the model can reason about it), stop when stop_reason is "end_turn". Use an iteration cap only as a safety-net ceiling, never as the primary termination signal.
decisions.anti: Parsing the assistant's text for phrases like "exploration complete", or relying on an iteration cap as the main stopping mechanism — both are unreliable next to the authoritative stop_reason field.

decisions.q: An agent has 18 tools and selects the wrong one. What's the most effective fix?
decisions.correct: Reduce to 4–5 tools per agent scoped to its role; distribute the rest across specialised subagents; add a scoped cross-role tool only for high-frequency hot paths.
decisions.anti: Making descriptions longer in isolation, switching to a larger model, or adding a routing classifier as the FIRST response. Selection reliability degrades with toolkit size — fix the structure first.

decisions.q: How to find every file that calls a deprecated function plus every test file for those callers?
decisions.correct: Grep for the function name first (content search → finds callers), then Glob for the matching test-file naming pattern (e.g. **/*.test.tsx). Grep then Glob.
decisions.anti: Glob-then-Grep — Glob can't search file CONTENTS, only paths; it cannot find function callers. Reading every file is the context-budget killer.

decisions.q: How to configure project-level MCP servers safely?
decisions.correct: .mcp.json at the repo root with ${ENV_VAR} for secrets — version-controlled for the team, each developer supplies their own credential in their environment.
decisions.anti: ~/.claude.json (personal only, not shared with the team) or hardcoding the credential value in .mcp.json (leaks via git history).

decisions.q: Edit fails with "old_string matches 3 locations" — what next?
decisions.correct: Widen old_string with surrounding context until it pins down ONE location, or use replace_all: true if every occurrence should change. Read + Write is the LAST resort.
decisions.anti: Immediately falling back to Read the whole file → Write the modified version. That burns tokens on the unchanged content and bypasses Edit's unique-match safety check.

decisions.q: A developer asks the agent to migrate a logging library across 30 files, with several equally valid integration approaches. What execution mode should the agent use?
decisions.correct: Plan mode first — explore the codebase, compare integration approaches, and design the migration strategy before touching any files; then switch to direct execution to apply the agreed approach file-by-file.
decisions.anti: Direct execution from the start (risks costly rework once hidden dependencies surface), or treating this like a single-file fix because each individual file change looks simple — the complexity here is architectural, not per-file.

domainsTested: D1: stop_reason-driven agentic loop for autonomous multi-step exploration
D2: Tool distribution (4–5 per agent; scoped cross-role)
D2: Grep vs Glob (content vs path search)
D2: MCP server configuration and ${ENV_VAR} secrets
D2: Edit recovery ordering — widen / replace_all / then Read+Write
D3: Plan mode for multi-file migrations with multiple valid approaches, then direct execution
strategy: Two facts that come up every time: (1) Grep is for file CONTENTS, Glob is for file PATHS — they're not interchangeable; (2) when Edit fails on non-unique match, widen the anchor or use replace_all FIRST — never default to Read + Write. This scenario also pulls in D1 (stop_reason for autonomous exploration loops) and D3 (plan mode when the task is already stated as architectural).

title: Claude Code for CI/CD
summary: Integrate Claude Code into continuous integration. Tests the -p flag, structured output, the Batches API trade-off, and session isolation between generator and reviewer.
focus: The -p flag for non-interactive CI
Structured output via --output-format json (+ --json-schema)
Batches API: when 50% cost savings vs latency makes sense
Separate sessions for generator vs reviewer

decisions.q: How to run Claude Code in a CI pipeline?
decisions.correct: Use `claude -p "…"` for non-interactive print mode — processes the prompt, writes output to stdout, exits without waiting for input.
decisions.anti: Running interactively (job hangs forever) or invented flags like --batch or CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true (those don't exist).

decisions.q: How to review code that Claude just generated, in the same pipeline?
decisions.correct: Use a SEPARATE `claude -p` invocation for review with no shared session context — a fresh instance evaluates the code on its own merits.
decisions.anti: Same-session self-review — the reviewing session retains the generator's reasoning and tends to confirm its own decisions rather than challenge them.

decisions.q: Nightly code-audit report: synchronous or Batches API?
decisions.correct: Message Batches API — ~50% cost savings, latency-tolerant (the report is read the next morning). Plan around the up-to-24-hour processing window; submit ≥24h before the deadline plus a safety buffer.
decisions.anti: Synchronous calls for non-urgent latency-tolerant work (pays 2× the cost for no benefit). Equally wrong: using Batches API for blocking pre-merge checks (developers can't wait 24h to merge).

decisions.q: How to make automated review output reliably parseable downstream?
decisions.correct: Use --output-format json combined with --json-schema enforcing a specific shape (e.g. file, line, severity, message) so the inline-PR-comment poster can read it without guessing.
decisions.anti: Parsing free-form prose with regex; or --output-format json WITHOUT a schema (fields can drift between runs).

domainsTested: D3: -p flag for non-interactive CI
D3: Independent-session review
D4: Batches API for non-blocking workloads only (Task 4.5 — cost/latency tradeoff)
D3: --output-format json + --json-schema for downstream automation
strategy: Three highly-testable facts: (1) -p for CI (the single most directly testable D3 fact); (2) ALWAYS a separate session for review; (3) the Batches API decision is technically Domain 4 (Task 4.5) content even though it shows up in a D3-flavoured CI scenario — cost/latency tradeoffs are tested there. Batches API is for non-blocking work, NEVER for blocking pre-merge checks.

title: Structured Data Extraction
summary: Build a structured-data extraction pipeline from unstructured documents. Tests JSON schema design, tool_choice modes, validation-retry loops, and few-shot prompting.
focus: JSON schema design (optional/nullable; "unclear"/"other")
tool_choice modes — auto vs any vs forced
Validation-retry with specific error feedback
Few-shot prompting for format consistency
Human review calibration: stratified sampling, accuracy by segment

decisions.q: How to guarantee structured JSON output when the document type is UNKNOWN across multiple schemas (invoice / receipt / contract)?
decisions.correct: tool_use with all three tools registered, and `tool_choice: { type: "any" }` — the model MUST call a tool but picks the schema that fits the document.
decisions.anti: tool_choice "auto" (model may return plain text — no guarantee) or forced selection of one specific tool (every document gets processed as that one type). Forced selection is for mandatory FIRST steps, not schema picking.

decisions.q: The model invents plausible-looking dates and amounts when fields are missing from the source. What schema change fixes this?
decisions.correct: Make the affected fields optional and nullable (type: ["string", "null"]; omit from required); add "unclear"/"other" enum values where classification is genuinely ambiguous.
decisions.anti: Keeping all fields required and adding a prompt instruction "do not hallucinate". Required-field pressure causes the fabrication; remove the pressure structurally.

decisions.q: What does tool_use with a JSON schema actually guarantee?
decisions.correct: STRUCTURAL conformance only — valid JSON, correct types, required fields present. SEMANTIC correctness (sums adding up, values in the right fields, not fabricated) needs separate validation + retry.
decisions.anti: Assuming output is correct because it parses. Schema-valid ≠ semantically correct.

decisions.q: Validation finds line_items summing to £450 against stated_total £500. How should the retry be constructed?
decisions.correct: Retry-with-error-feedback containing THREE pieces: the original document, the failed extraction, and the SPECIFIC validation error ("line items sum to £450 but stated_total is £500 — likely missed a line item").
decisions.anti: Generic "there were errors, please try again". With no signal, the model usually reproduces the same mistake.

decisions.q: Your extraction pipeline reports 97% overall accuracy, so you plan to stop routing high-confidence extractions to human review. What should you check first?
decisions.correct: Break accuracy down by document type and field — an aggregate 97% can mask a specific document type or field performing far worse. Use stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions to keep measuring real-world error rates and catch novel error patterns before fully automating.
decisions.anti: Trusting the aggregate 97% figure at face value, or routing review purely by a single global confidence threshold without first calibrating it against a labelled validation set.

domainsTested: D4: tool_choice — "any" for unknown schemas, forced for mandatory first steps, auto for conversational
D4: Schema design — optional/nullable, "unclear"/"other" enums
D4: tool_use guarantees structure, not semantics
D4: Retry-with-error-feedback with specific validation context
D5: Aggregate-accuracy trap — validate by document type/field before automating review away
strategy: Two specific traps: (1) for guaranteed structured output on UNKNOWN document types, the answer is tool_choice "any" — not forced selection of a single tool; (2) tool_use ≠ semantic correctness — pair it with explicit validation. Always retry with the SPECIFIC error, never with "try again". And don't trust a single aggregate accuracy number — segment it by document type and field before reducing human review (D5).
